solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Slippery item beginning to bother a relative’s family (6,4)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: the beginning of 'bother' is its first letter

blocks.note: nana is a grandmother; the possessive adds S

annotation.surface: Something slippery threatens to cause trouble for a relative's household.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive S runs straight into KIN, so the answer's word break falls inside a piece. Nana is an informal word for grandmother.
annotation.definitionFit: A banana skin is the classic thing to slip on, and figuratively a pitfall.

entries.clue: Lady Godiva’s attire represented a British duty (8,4)

indicatorNotes.represented: re-presented: the letters are presented again in a new order

annotation.surface: Lady Godiva's naked ride is framed as a patriotic obligation.
annotation.walkthrough: Lady Godiva is the legendary noblewoman who rode naked through Coventry, so her 'attire' was none at all.
annotation.definitionFit: A birthday suit is bare skin, which is all Lady Godiva wore.

entries.clue: Masked warrior partially hidden in Jakarta (5)

indicatorNotes.partially: only part of the following words is used

annotation.surface: A masked fighter lies half-concealed somewhere in Jakarta.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hidden' looks like the instruction, but it is fodder: its last letter starts the answer, and 'partially' does the work.
annotation.definitionFit: Ninjas were Japanese covert fighters, traditionally shown masked.

entries.clue: Sister needed up north primarily (3)

indicatorNotes.primarily: take the prime, or first, letter of each word

annotation.surface: A sister is required in the north of the country.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a request for a nurse or nun somewhere up north; only 'primarily' says to read the three initials instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Nuns are addressed by the title Sister, so the definition names one by her form of address.

entries.clue: Pacific islander as upset over complaint (6)

indicatorNotes.upset: in a down clue, upset turns the letters upside down, so they read backwards

annotation.surface: An islander is annoyed about some grievance.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'over' also means on top of, so the upturned AS sits above MOAN.
annotation.definitionFit: Samoans come from Samoa, in the South Pacific.

entries.clue: Position in prison for certain kind of crime? (6,3)

annotation.surface: Someone asks what post a convict holds, and what crime it suggests.
annotation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the reverse order of the clue: JOB is 'Position', written first, but it ends the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An inside job is a crime committed with help from someone within the organisation robbed.

entries.clue: Aspire to change ancient empire (6)

annotation.surface: Someone hopes to reform an old empire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aspire' sits first as if it were the verb of the sentence, but it is only six letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Persia was the ancient empire centred on modern Iran.

entries.clue: Dance is with editor to secure perfect location? (8,4)

blocks.note: a prom is a formal dance
to land a deal is to secure it

annotation.surface: A dance and an editor combine to book the ideal venue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Secure' reads as a verb acting on the location, but it is simply LAND. The question mark flags the definition as loose: a promised land is ideal, not literally perfect.
annotation.definitionFit: The promised land is a longed-for place of happiness, from the land promised to Abraham.

entries.clue: Period of time immediately before altercation (3-2)

blocks.note: the lead-up stretch before an event, as before an election
a quarrel or brush with someone, e.g. with the police

annotation.surface: The moments just before a fight broke out.
annotation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay here: the surface fuses the two meanings into one story of the minutes before a scuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: Run-in covers both the approach to an event and an argument or confrontation.

entries.clue: Assemble most of currency for rubber? (7)

indicatorNotes.most of: take all but the last letter

annotation.surface: Gathering nearly all your cash to buy an eraser.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' looks like an eraser or a tyre; the question mark says it is one who rubs.
annotation.definitionFit: A masseur rubs people's muscles for a living.

entries.clue: Had learnt to move around central region (9)

indicatorNotes.to move around: the letters move into new places

annotation.surface: Someone had learnt to travel about the middle of the country.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a traveller's progress; 'to move around' is the instruction, and the fodder is the first two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A heartland is the central, most important part of a region.

entries.clue: Money manager, initially tight, certain to cut back (9)

indicatorNotes.to cut: SURE cuts into REAR, splitting it

annotation.surface: A tight-fisted money manager is determined to make cuts.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make 'cut back' look like a spending cut; in fact 'cut' is the container instruction and 'back' is the word being cut into.
annotation.definitionFit: Treasurer is the title in clubs and companies for the officer who looks after the funds, a fair gloss as a money manager.

entries.clue: Total is small? Let me think … (3)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
um is the sound of hesitation

annotation.surface: Someone pauses to decide whether a total is small.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis and question mark make it look like hesitant speech; 'Let me think …' is exactly that hesitation, written as UM.
annotation.definitionFit: Sum and total are plain noun synonyms: the result of adding numbers up.

entries.clue: Disney princess returns outside one part of church (5)

indicatorNotes.returns: the name comes back, reading backwards
indicatorNotes.outside: the reversed name goes outside the letter for one

annotation.surface: A Disney princess comes back to stand outside a church.
annotation.walkthrough: ELSA turned around is ASLE, and I slips in after its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The aisle is the passage between the pews of a church.

entries.clue: Try hard with new rivets (6)

indicatorNotes.new: the letters are made into something new

annotation.surface: A worker makes an effort with fresh rivets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New' passes for an ordinary adjective describing the rivets; it is one of the commonest anagram signals.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: striving is making a strenuous effort.

entries.clue: Trousers belonging to Sibelius, perhaps? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: the second definition is possessive: JEAN'S, whose apostrophe the grid drops

blocks.note: the Finnish composer's first name, made possessive; 'perhaps' says he is one example

annotation.surface: A pair of trousers that once belonged to the Finnish composer.
annotation.walkthrough: Sibelius's first name was Jean, so his things are JEAN'S. Sibelius is the surname solvers know, which hides the first name.
annotation.definitionFit: Jeans are trousers, and Jean's means owned by a Jean.

entries.clue: Setter put into vehicle with a picture taker (6)

indicatorNotes.put into: to put something into a container places it inside, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the setter refers to themselves as me

annotation.surface: The setter climbs into a car with someone taking photos.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Setter' means the person who wrote the clue, so it gives ME, not a dog or a jelly.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the device that takes photographs, described by what it does.

entries.clue: Title of father shortened (3)

indicatorNotes.shortened: a shortened word has been cut down, here by losing its final letter

blocks.note: SIRE, a father, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A father's title has been abbreviated.
annotation.walkthrough: Sire is an old word for a father, still used of horses; drop its E.
annotation.definitionFit: The honorific used for a knight or baronet, and as a polite form of address.

entries.clue: Celebrity committee is at sea, right? (9)

blocks.note: a board is a governing committee

annotation.surface: A celebrity asks whether a committee is confused.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' looks like it means bewildered; with 'right' it becomes the definition, right as sailors say it.
annotation.definitionFit: Starboard is the right-hand side of a ship, facing forward.

entries.clue: Car with zero sound (5)

blocks.note: Audi is a make of car

annotation.surface: A car that makes no noise at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Car' is a make, not the general word, and the definition is the last word.
annotation.definitionFit: Used as a noun for sound, especially recorded or broadcast sound, as in a film's soundtrack.

entries.clue: Opposite of fashionable poetry (7)

annotation.surface: Something is the opposite of trendy poems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opposite of' reads as one phrase; 'of' is only a link, and 'Opposite' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun synonym from logic and maths: reversing a relation gives its counterpart, as with the reciprocal of a fraction.

entries.clue: Foolhardy hero holding back monster (5)

indicatorNotes.holding: the words hold the answer inside them

annotation.surface: A reckless hero keeps a monster at bay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Holding back' reads as restraining the monster; it is two instructions, hide and reverse. ARDYH read backwards is HYDRA.
annotation.definitionFit: The Hydra was the many-headed monster killed by Hercules.

entries.clue: Owns shears regularly (3)

blocks.note: sHeArS: the second, fourth and sixth letters

annotation.surface: Someone possesses shears that they use routinely.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' passes for an adverb about using the shears, but it says to take every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to possess something, in the present tense to match 'Owns'.

entries.clue: Dad borrows terribly big chopper (10)

annotation.surface: Father helps himself to a huge axe without asking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' suggests an axe or a helicopter; here it is a sword.
annotation.definitionFit: A broadsword is a large, broad-bladed sword for cutting blows.
